🍎 Lesson plan · 🌱 Basics · Lesson 1

Lesson plan: What is AI?

What artificial intelligence really is — and what it isn't.

By the end of the lesson, students can

  • explain in their own words what AI is;
  • tell a program that follows hand-written rules from a system that learned from examples;
  • explain why all AI today is narrow, and what general AI (AGI) would be.

Warm-up

Name one thing from your day so far that you think uses AI. What makes you think so?

Write the answers on the board without correcting them. At the end of the lesson, sort the list together: AI, or just fixed rules?

Reading

Students read the lesson “What is AI?”. Students look for the difference between following rules and learning from examples, and for the year the term “artificial intelligence” was invented.

Activity: Mini-lab “AI or not AI?”

  1. Students work in pairs and scroll to the mini-lab at the end of lesson 1.
  2. Before clicking anything, each pair writes down its guess for every example: AI or not AI.
  3. Then they choose the answers on screen and read every explanation.
  4. Each pair picks the example they argued about most and prepares one sentence: what clue shows that a system learned from data?

For students who finish early

Fast finishers invent two examples of their own, one with AI and one without, and swap them with another pair.

Discussion questions

  • A calculator always gives the right answer, but it isn't AI. Why not?
  • Is a chatbot that can talk about almost anything an example of general AI? Why, or why not?
  • Which AI in your life would you miss most if it stopped working tomorrow?
  • Experts disagree about whether general AI will ever exist. Why is it so hard to predict?

Exit ticket

Write your own one-sentence definition of AI, and give one example from your life.

Quick check. A chess program can beat any human champion, but it can't recognise a cat in a photo. What kind of AI is it?
Right answer: Narrow AI: it is built for one kind of task

Easier and harder

Easier. Before the reading, cut the worksheet's sorting task into cards to sort into two piles, and give a sentence starter for the definition: “AI is when a computer…”.

Harder. Students find a device at home or at school that is sold as “smart” and decide, with reasons, whether it learns from data or only follows fixed rules.
